column2: Also on the authority of ʿUmar (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him), who said:

While we were sitting with the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) one day, there appeared before us a man whose clothes were exceedingly white and whose hair was exceedingly black. No trace of travel could be seen on him, and none of us knew him.

He came and sat down by the Prophet (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace), rested his knees against his knees, placed his palms on his thighs, and said: O Muḥammad, tell me about Islam.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Islam is that you testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish the prayer, give the zakāh, fast Ramaḍān, and make pilgrimage to the House if you are able to find a way to it.
He said: You have spoken truly. We were amazed at him: he asks him and then confirms him! He said: Then tell me about faith (īmān).
He said: That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, and that you believe in the decree (qadar), its good and its bad. He said: You have spoken truly.
He said: Then tell me about excellence (iḥsān).
He said: That you worship Allah as though you see Him; and though you do not see Him, He surely sees you.
In the answer about excellence the printed text reads تبعد (“distance”), evidently a misprint for تعبد (“worship”).

He said: Then tell me about the Hour. He said: The one asked about it knows no more than the one asking. He said: Then tell me about its signs. He said: That the slave-woman gives birth to her mistress, and that you see the barefoot, unclothed, destitute shepherds of sheep competing in raising tall buildings.
Then he left, and I stayed a long while. Then he said: O ʿUmar, do you know who the questioner was?
I said: Allah and His Messenger know best. He said: That was Jibrīl, who came to you to teach you your religion.” Reported by Muslim.
Rajul (“a man”): an angel in the form of a man.
“No trace … could be seen (lā yurā) on him”: with the yāʾ, the letter dotted twice below, carrying ḍammah, according to the well-known reading.
Some narrated it with the nūn carrying fatḥah (“we did not see”), and both are correct.
“On his thighs”: on the thighs of the Prophet ﷺ, as is understood from the narration of al-Nasāʾī.

“That you testify that there is no god but Allah”: the meaning of this statement is made clear by what is in the other narration, from Abū Hurayrah, with the wording: “That you worship Allah and do not associate anything with Him.”
“And that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah”: creation must believe him, obey him in what he commands and refrain from what he forbids.
“Establish the prayer”: the prescribed prayer.
As for voluntary prayer, although it is one of the duties of Islam, it is not one of its pillars.
The same applies to what is beyond the obligatory in zakāh, fasting and Ḥajj.
“Give the zakāh”: the obligatory zakāh, to those entitled to it.
“Fast Ramaḍān”: refrain during its days from whatever breaks the fast, with an intention.
“Make pilgrimage to the House”: go to it to perform the rites counted among the pillars of Islam. “If you are able to find a way to it”: that is, provisions and a mount.

“We were amazed at him: he asks him and then confirms him”: because what the Prophet ﷺ gave as an answer could be known only from him, and this questioner was not someone known to have met the Prophet ﷺ and heard from him.
Moreover, he asked in the manner of someone who knew what he was asking about,
for otherwise he would not have told him that he had spoken truly.
“That you believe in Allah”: that He is described by the attributes of perfection and free of the attributes of deficiency,
without partner.
“His angels”: that they are as Allah described them: “honoured servants; they do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command” [al-Anbiyāʾ 21:26–27].
“His books”: that they are the speech of Allah and that what they contain is true.
“His messengers”: that they are truthful and that they conveyed everything Allah commanded them to convey.

“The Last Day”: the Day of Resurrection, with all that it includes of the resurrection, the reckoning, the Balance, the Bridge, Paradise, the Fire and the other matters established by authentic texts.

“And that you believe in the decree, its good and its bad”: that Allah knew the measures of all things and their times before bringing them into being, and then brought into being what His knowledge had already determined would come to be.

So everything that comes to be proceeds from His knowledge, power and will, whether good or bad; and that you know that what has befallen you was not going to miss you, and what has missed you was not going to befall you.
“And though you do not see Him, He surely sees you”: that is, continue to worship with excellence, for He sees you.
“About the Hour”: when it will be established.
What is meant by the Hour is the Day of Resurrection.
“The one asked about it knows no more than the one asking”: neither I nor you know its time; rather, it is among the things whose knowledge Allah has kept to Himself.
Amārātuhā (“its signs”): with fatḥah on the hamzah; its indications.

“That the slave-woman gives birth to her mistress (rabbatahā)”: rabbatahā means her mistress. This has been explained as referring to the spread of Islam and its people's taking control of the lands of shirk, so that taking concubines becomes common,

and the child of a slave-woman by her master has the standing of her master, being honoured through his father. It has also been explained as referring to widespread undutifulness, until a child treats his mother as a master treats his slave-woman, humiliating her with insults, beatings and making her serve him.

The ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar preferred this, saying: because the context indicates that what is meant is a state of affairs that, besides indicating the corruption of conditions, is unusual. He mentioned that taking concubines already existed when this was said, so interpreting the hadith as referring to it is questionable.
Al-ḥufāh (“the barefoot”): plural of ḥāfin,
one who wears no sandals.
Al-ʿurāh (“the unclothed”): plural of ʿārin, one who has nothing on his body.
Al-ʿālah (“the destitute”): the poor.
Riʿāʾ al-shāʾ (“shepherds of sheep”): with kasrah on the rāʾ;
their keepers. Al-shāʾ is the plural of shāh (a sheep).
“Competing in raising tall buildings”: vying with one another in making their buildings tall and boasting of having more of them.
Fa-labithtu (“and I stayed”): I remained after he had left.
Malīyyan (“a long while”): with the yāʾ doubled;
a long time, as made clear by the narration of al-Nasāʾī and al-Tirmidhī: “I stayed three [days].”
“To teach you your religion”: the universal principles of your religion.
Making one's clothes and appearance good and being clean when entering upon people of virtue, for Jibrīl came teaching people by his appearance as well as his words.
Gentleness with the questioner and bringing him near, so that he can ask without feeling constrained or intimidated.
Asking a scholar something the questioner already knows, so that the listener may learn it.
An explanation of Islam, faith and excellence, and calling them all “religion”.

Distinguishing between what is named Islam and what is named faith, since in the hadith Islam was made the name for outward deeds and faith the name for inward ones. The scholars have reconciled this with what the mass-transmitted texts indicate, that faith is both speech and action,

by saying that when either of these two names is used alone, the other is included in it, and on its own it indicates what the other indicates on its own; but when they are paired together, one of them indicates part of what it would indicate on its own, and the other indicates the rest.

The obligation to believe in the decree. It has two degrees. The first is believing that Allah's knowledge preceded what His servants would do of good and evil, obedience and disobedience, before He created them and brought them into being,

and who among them is of the people of Paradise and who among them is of the people of the Fire; that He prepared reward and punishment for them as recompense for their deeds before creating and forming them; and that He wrote that down with Him and recorded it.
The second is that Allah created all the actions of His servants, whether disbelief or faith, obedience or disobedience,
and willed them from them. Nevertheless, the decree may not be used as an excuse for sins.
The time of the establishment of the Hour is among the things whose knowledge Allah has kept to Himself.
When a scholar is asked about something he does not know, he should state plainly that he does not know it,

and not use expressions that waver between giving an answer and admitting that he does not know. This does not diminish him; rather, it is evidence of his scrupulousness and fear of Allah, and of his not making a show of knowledge he does not have.
Among the signs of the Hour is the overturning of affairs, so that the one who was reared becomes the one who rears, and the lowly becomes high.
Asking a good question is called knowledge and teaching, because the Prophet ﷺ said of Jibrīl, “to teach you your religion”, even though nothing came from him except questions.
